claim: The P. berghei limp gene (PBANKA_0605800) is 1194 basepairs long and comprises six exons and five introns.
source: The Plasmodium berghei limp gene (1194 bp) is composed of six exons (shaded bars) and five introns (lines).
evidence: The gene structure is described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LIMP is encoded by a gene that produces a protein of 110 amino acids with a 22 amino acid long signal peptide.
source: The gene (Figure 1A) comprises six exons and five introns (this organisation is conserved throughout the genus) and encodes a protein of 110 amino acids (aa) with a 22 aa long signal peptide (Figure 1B) and a molecular weight of 13 kDa.
evidence: The protein characteristics are directly stated in the text based on gene analysis.

claim: LIMP has a molecular weight of 13 kDa.
source: The gene (Figure 1A) comprises six exons and five introns (this organisation is conserved throughout the genus) and encodes a protein of 110 amino acids (aa) with a 22 aa long signal peptide (Figure 1B) and a molecular weight of 13 kDa.
evidence: The molecular weight is calculated from the protein sequence.

claim: Ab initio protein structure predictions indicate that LIMP (I23 to G110) consists of three beta sheets opposed to two α-helices.
source: Ab initio protein structure predictions (Combet et al., 2000; Xu and Zhang, 2012) indicate that LIMP (I23 to G110) consists of three beta sheets opposed to two α-helices (Figure 1C).
evidence: The structure is predicted using computational methods cited in the text.

claim: LIMP is highly conserved among various Plasmodium species.
source: LIMP is highly conserved among the various Plasmodium species (Figure 1B; www.plasmodb.org) (Aurrecoechea et al., 2009)
evidence: Conservation is demonstrated through sequence alignment and database analysis.

claim: LIMP homologs in related apicomplexan parasites have homology focused on a 22 amino acid proline-rich region adjacent to the signal peptide.
source: similarly short proteins are present in related apicomplexan parasites, where the homology is focused on a 22 amino acid proline-rich region adjacent to the signal peptide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Sequence alignment shows conserved regions in related parasites.

claim: limp mRNA is enriched in an RNA-immunoprecipitation (RIP) of CITH.
source: limp was found downregulated in a gene knock-out for the translational repressor DOZI and its mRNA enriched in an RNA-immunoprecipitation (RIP) of CITH (Mair et al., 2006, 2010; Guerreiro et al., 2014)
evidence: RIP experiments demonstrate association with CITH protein.

claim: limp was found downregulated in a gene knock-out for the translational repressor DOZI.
source: limp was found downregulated in a gene knock-out for the translational repressor DOZI and its mRNA enriched in an RNA-immunoprecipitation (RIP) of CITH (Mair et al., 2006, 2010; Guerreiro et al., 2014)
evidence: Gene expression analysis in DOZI knockout parasites shows downregulation.

claim: limp mRNA is kept translationally repressed in female gametocytes until activated during ookinete development, or later.
source: limp was found downregulated in a gene knock-out for the translational repressor DOZI and its mRNA enriched in an RNA-immunoprecipitation (RIP) of CITH (Mair et al., 2006, 2010; Guerreiro et al., 2014), suggesting that limp mRNA is kept translationally repressed in female gametocytes until activated during ookinete development, or later.
evidence: The translational repression is inferred from DOZI and CITH association data.

claim: LIMP protein is not expressed in asexual stage parasites or gametocytes.
source: We found no protein expression in asexual stage parasites or gametocytes
evidence: Immunofluorescence assays show no protein expression in these stages.

claim: limp::gfp is translated in the ookinete stage.
source: limp::gfp is translated in the ookinete stage and its expression is visible in crystalloids (transient and putative storage organelles of the ookinete) (Dessens et al., 2011) and the surface
evidence: Live imaging and immunofluorescence show protein expression in ookinetes.

claim: LIMP::GFP expression is visible in crystalloids and the surface of ookinetes.
source: limp::gfp is translated in the ookinete stage and its expression is visible in crystalloids (transient and putative storage organelles of the ookinete) (Dessens et al., 2011) and the surface
evidence: Microscopy images show localization in crystalloids and surface.

claim: LIMP::GFP produces a faint 'dusting' on the surface of midgut and salivary gland sporozoites.
source: the protein produced a faint 'dusting' on the surface of midgut and salivary gland sporozoites (Figure 1E; see also Figure 4).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging shows speckled surface distribution.

claim: limp mRNA was not detected in asexual blood stages.
source: In agreement with previously published results (Otto et al., 2014), limp mRNA was not detected in asexual blood stages
evidence: RT-PCR analysis shows absence of mRNA in asexual stages.

claim: limp mRNA is present in gametocytes while protein is not.
source: mRNA is however present in gametocytes (while protein is not) and in ookinetes (where protein is present) (Figure 1F)
evidence: RT-PCR shows mRNA presence while IFA shows no protein in gametocytes.

claim: limp mRNA is present in ookinetes where protein is also present.
source: mRNA is however present in gametocytes (while protein is not) and in ookinetes (where protein is present) (Figure 1F)
evidence: RT-PCR and IFA show both mRNA and protein in ookinetes.

claim: limp is translationally repressed and maternally provided to the developing ookinete.
source: this is consistent with limp being translationally repressed and maternally provided to the developing ookinete.
evidence: The pattern of mRNA presence without protein in gametocytes and protein appearance in ookinetes supports maternal provision.

claim: Western blot analysis of ookinete material confirmed expression of a GFP fusion protein of the expected size.
source: Western blot analysis of ookinete material confirmed expression of a GFP fusion protein of the expected size (Figure 1G).
evidence: Western blot shows a band at the expected molecular weight for LIMP::GFP.

claim: Parasites expressing LIMP::GFP showed no defects in liver stage development in vitro.
source: Parasites expressing LIMP::GFP showed no defects in liver stage development in vitro nor during transmission to the rodent host by mosquito bite (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: In vitro hepatocyte infection assays show normal EEF development.

claim: Parasites expressing LIMP::GFP showed no defects during transmission to the rodent host by mosquito bite.
source: Parasites expressing LIMP::GFP showed no defects in liver stage development in vitro nor during transmission to the rodent host by mosquito bite (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Mosquito bite transmission experiments show normal blood-stage infection.

claim: The absence of LIMP does not affect asexual blood-stage development.
source: The absence of LIMP did not affect asexual blood-stage development, gametocyte numbers nor female to male ratios (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: FACS analysis shows normal parasitemia in Δlimp parasites.

claim: The absence of LIMP does not affect gametocyte numbers.
source: The absence of LIMP did not affect asexual blood-stage development, gametocyte numbers nor female to male ratios (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: FACS analysis shows normal gametocytemia in Δlimp parasites.

claim: The absence of LIMP does not affect female to male gametocyte ratios.
source: The absence of LIMP did not affect asexual blood-stage development, gametocyte numbers nor female to male ratios (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: FACS analysis shows normal sex ratios in Δlimp parasites.

claim: The capacity of Δlimp parasites to produce ookinetes was comparable to that of wildtype lines.
source: the capacity of Δlimp parasites to produce ookinetes was comparable to that of wildtype (WT) lines; in vitro zygote to ookinete conversion rates ranged from 55% to 91% (Figure 2A).
evidence: In vitro ookinete conversion assays show similar rates for WT and Δlimp.

claim: In vitro zygote to ookinete conversion rates for Δlimp parasites ranged from 55% to 91%.
source: the capacity of Δlimp parasites to produce ookinetes was comparable to that of wildtype (WT) lines; in vitro zygote to ookinete conversion rates ranged from 55% to 91% (Figure 2A).
evidence: Ookinete conversion assays provide quantitative data.

claim: Following a mosquito blood meal, infection rates (oocyst numbers per mosquito) were reduced below 50% in Δlimp parasites.
source: However, following a mosquito blood meal, infection rates (oocyst numbers per mosquito) were reduced below 50% (Figure 2B)
evidence: Oocyst counts in infected mosquitoes show significant reduction.

claim: The number of oocyst-derived midgut sporozoites per oocyst remained unchanged in Δlimp parasites.
source: while the number of oocyst-derived midgut sporozoites per oocyst remained unchanged (Figure 2C)
evidence: Sporozoite counts per oocyst show no difference between WT and Δlimp.

claim: Ookinete development does not require LIMP.
source: ookinete development and oocyst sporulation therefore do not require LIMP.
evidence: Normal ookinete conversion rates and sporozoites per oocyst indicate LIMP is not required for these processes.

claim: Oocyst sporulation does not require LIMP.
source: ookinete development and oocyst sporulation therefore do not require LIMP.
evidence: Normal sporozoites per oocyst indicate LIMP is not required for sporulation.

claim: Δlimp sporozoites did not significantly accumulate in the haemolymph.
source: Δlimp sporozoites did not significantly accumulate in the haemolymph (Figure 2D)
evidence: Haemolymph sporozoite counts show no significant difference from WT.

claim: Δlimp sporozoites showed a 10-fold reduction in salivary gland invasion.
source: but showed a 10-fold reduction in salivary gland invasion (Figure 2E).
evidence: Salivary gland sporozoite counts show dramatic reduction in Δlimp parasites.

claim: LIMP plays a role during mosquito midgut colonisation by the ookinete.
source: Our results demonstrate a role for LIMP during mosquito midgut colonisation by the ookinete
evidence: 50% reduction in oocyst numbers demonstrates a role in midgut colonization.

claim: LIMP has a crucial function during salivary gland invasion.
source: and a crucial function for the protein during salivary gland invasion
evidence: 10-fold reduction in salivary gland sporozoites demonstrates crucial function.

claim: LIMP is not required for ookinete development.
source: but not for development; neither ookinete nor sporozoite formation were affected by the absence of LIMP.
evidence: Normal ookinete conversion rates indicate LIMP is not required for development.

claim: LIMP is not required for sporozoite formation.
source: but not for development; neither ookinete nor sporozoite formation were affected by the absence of LIMP.
evidence: Normal sporozoites per oocyst indicate LIMP is not required for sporozoite formation.

claim: WT-infected mice established normal blood-stage parasitaemias after i.v. injection of 3,500 salivary gland sporozoites.
source: WT-infected mice established normal blood-stage parasitaemias, while KO-infected mice never did.
evidence: Blood-stage parasitemia monitoring shows normal infection in WT.

claim: Δlimp-infected mice never established blood-stage parasitaemias after i.v. injection of 3,500 salivary gland sporozoites.
source: WT-infected mice established normal blood-stage parasitaemias, while KO-infected mice never did.
evidence: Blood-stage parasitemia monitoring shows no infection in Δlimp.

claim: Mice injected i.v. with Δlimp salivary gland sporozoites showed no parasite load in the liver at 44 hr post-infection when determined by qPCR.
source: Mice injected i.v. with Δlimp salivary gland sporozoites showed no parasite load in the liver at 44 hr post-infection (p.i.) when determined by qPCR of the P. berghei ANKA 18S gene (Figure 2G)
evidence: qPCR analysis shows no detectable parasite 18S rRNA in liver.

claim: Δlimp mutants failed to invade the liver.
source: corroborating the notion that mutants had failed to invade the liver.
evidence: Absence of liver parasite load and blood-stage infection indicates failure to invade liver.

claim: Δlimp salivary gland sporozoites did not establish exoerythrocytic forms (EEFs) inside Huh7 hepatoma cells.
source: In vitro hepatocyte infection assays supported the in vivo data; Δlimp salivary gland sporozoites did not establish exoerythrocytic forms (EEFs) inside Huh7 hepatoma cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: In vitro infection assays show no EEF formation by Δlimp sporozoites.

claim: Δlimp sporozoites showed a complete failure to traverse hepatocytes when determined by FACS analysis.
source: limp KO sporozoites showed a complete failure to traverse hepatocytes when determined by FACS analysis; the percentage of Dextran+ host cells (the polysaccharide enters through cell membrane injury sites caused by invading sporozoites) was not different from levels obtained from cells incubated with non-infected mosquito salivary gland material (Figure 3A).
evidence: Dextran uptake assay shows no cell traversal by Δlimp sporozoites.

claim: Δlimp sporozoites showed a clear defect in adherence to Huh7 cells.
source: Mutant sporozoites also showed a clear defect in adherence to Huh7 cells (Figure 3B)
evidence: Adhesion assays show reduced attachment of Δlimp sporozoites to hepatocytes.

claim: Δlimp sporozoites showed greatly reduced hepatocyte invasion.
source: together with greatly reduced hepatocyte invasion (Figure 3C)
evidence: Invasion assays show minimal invasion by Δlimp sporozoites.

claim: Δlimp parasites were severely impaired in gliding motility.
source: KO parasites were severely impaired in gliding motility, evident by the large number of completely immotile parasites as well as the number of gliding trails of the few moving ones (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: CSP trail assays show very few trails produced by Δlimp sporozoites.

claim: Δlimp parasites have normal morphology with no ultrastructural defects in key components of the gliding motility machinery.
source: Morphologically, KO parasites are normal. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) studies of Δlimp sporozoites revealed no ultrastructural defects in key components of the gliding motility machinery. The arrangement of the plasma membrane (PM), inner membrane complex (IMC), subpellicular microtubules as well as secretory vesicles (micronemes and rhoptries) was unchanged (Figure 3F).
evidence: TEM images show normal cellular structures in Δlimp sporozoites.

claim: Some Δlimp sporozoites can invade the mosquito salivary glands.
source: As expected, Δlimp sporozoites were found within the mosquito's salivary gland parenchyma, confirming that some mutants can invade the salivary glands and are not merely attached to the outer surface of the glands facing the haemocoel (Figure 3G).
evidence: TEM images show Δlimp sporozoites inside salivary gland tissue.

claim: LIMP::GFP localises to the sporozoite surface.
source: When we performed IFAs on limp::gfp sporozoites recovered from salivary glands, fluorescence was found in a dusted, speckled distribution along the entire length of the parasite (Figure 1E and Figure 4A). LIMP::GFP was detectable both with and without Triton X-100 permeabilisation (Figure 4A), a clear indication for parasite cell surface positioning of LIMP in a manner resembling TRAP (which is secreted from micronemes) and CSP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: IFA with and without permeabilization shows surface localization.

claim: LIMP::GFP is detectable both with and without Triton X-100 permeabilisation.
source: LIMP::GFP was detectable both with and without Triton X-100 permeabilisation (Figure 4A), a clear indication for parasite cell surface positioning of LIMP in a manner resembling TRAP (which is secreted from micronemes) and CSP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Detection without permeabilization indicates surface accessibility.

claim: The staining patterns of tagged LIMP in limp::gfp, mcherry::limp, and limp::myc transgenic lines were identical.
source: The staining patterns of tagged LIMP in all three transgenic lines was identical (Figure 4A), showing that trafficking of tagged LIMP does not alter with tag size nor position (N- versus C-terminus)
evidence: IFA images show similar speckled surface distribution in all three tagged lines.

claim: Trafficking of tagged LIMP does not alter with tag size nor position (N- versus C-terminus).
source: The staining patterns of tagged LIMP in all three transgenic lines was identical (Figure 4A), showing that trafficking of tagged LIMP does not alter with tag size nor position (N- versus C-terminus)
evidence: Identical localization patterns across different tags indicate trafficking is not affected.

claim: 76% of gold particles in immuno-EM were associated with the parasite plasma membrane.
source: Using an immuno-electron microscopy (immuno-EM) approach (Figure 4B), we corroborated LIMP::GFP localisation in three independent staining experiments with three different parasite samples. Seventy-six percent of gold particles (from a total of 281) were associated with the parasite PM, 11% outside of parasites; 13% were intracellular although not clearly associated with any specific organelle.
evidence: Quantification of gold particle positions in immuno-EM images.

claim: 11% of gold particles in immuno-EM were outside of parasites.
source: Seventy-six percent of gold particles (from a total of 281) were associated with the parasite PM, 11% outside of parasites; 13% were intracellular although not clearly associated with any specific organelle.
evidence: Quantification of gold particle positions in immuno-EM images.

claim: 13% of gold particles in immuno-EM were intracellular although not clearly associated with any specific organelle.
source: Seventy-six percent of gold particles (from a total of 281) were associated with the parasite PM, 11% outside of parasites; 13% were intracellular although not clearly associated with any specific organelle.
evidence: Quantification of gold particle positions in immuno-EM images.

claim: The vast majority of Δlimp haemolymph sporozoites were found floating in the medium, unable to attach to the glass bottom of a 96-well plate.
source: Again, exceptionally few gene deletion sporozoites showed normal circular movement while the vast majority were found floating in the medium (Figure 4C), unable to attach to the glass bottom of a 96-well plate.
evidence: Live motility assays show most Δlimp sporozoites are non-adherent.

claim: limp::gfp haemolymph sporozoites displayed a normal distribution of gliding motility patterns.
source: As expected, the limp::gfp haemolymph sporozoite population displayed a normal distribution of gliding motility patterns (Figure 4C).
evidence: Live motility assays show similar movement patterns to WT.

claim: limp::gfp sporozoites move significantly slower than WT sporozoites.
source: But when we analysed the speed of productively moving WT and limp::gfp sporozoites we found, surprisingly, limp::gfp sporozoites to move significantly slower (Figure 4D)
evidence: Quantitative analysis of sporozoite speed shows significant reduction in limp::gfp.

claim: limp::gfp salivary gland sporozoites produce normal numbers of CSP trails.
source: despite limp::gfp salivary gland sporozoites producing normal numbers of CSP trails (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: CSP trail assays show similar trail numbers for WT and limp::gfp.

claim: The presence of high concentrations of anti-GFP antibodies did not affect CSP shedding by limp::gfp sporozoites.
source: The presence of high concentrations of anti-GFP antibodies (potentially targeting LIMP::GFP) nor control IgGs affected CSP shedding (Figure 4E)
evidence: CSP trail assays with antibodies show no change in trail formation.

claim: Control IgGs did not affect CSP shedding by limp::gfp sporozoites.
source: The presence of high concentrations of anti-GFP antibodies (potentially targeting LIMP::GFP) nor control IgGs affected CSP shedding (Figure 4E)
evidence: CSP trail assays with control IgGs show no change in trail formation.

claim: Anti-GFP antibodies did not affect in vitro hepatocyte invasion by limp::gfp sporozoites.
source: or in vitro hepatocyte invasion by limp::gfp sporozoites (Figure 4G)
evidence: Invasion assays with antibodies show no change in invasion rates.

claim: Control IgGs did not affect in vitro hepatocyte invasion by limp::gfp sporozoites.
source: or in vitro hepatocyte invasion by limp::gfp sporozoites (Figure 4G)
evidence: Invasion assays with control IgGs show no change in invasion rates.

claim: Anti-TRAP antibodies have no effect on gliding motility.
source: mimicking a published TRAP study showing no effect of anti-TRAP antibodies on gliding motility (Gantt et al., 2000)
evidence: Published study cited shows anti-TRAP antibodies do not block motility.

claim: Anti-CSP antibodies stopped sporozoite motility in vitro and blocked hepatocyte invasion in vivo.
source: while anti-CSP antibodies stopped sporozoite motility in vitro and blocked hepatocyte invasion in vivo (Stewart et al., 1986).
evidence: Published study cited shows anti-CSP antibodies block motility and invasion.

claim: GFP-tagged LIMP is not shed from the parasite surface during gliding, or is shed at levels below the detection limit.
source: To this end, we coated microscope slides with anti-GFP antibodies used for sporozoite immunofluorescence. No gliding trails were detected in this assay, suggesting that GFP-tagged LIMP is not shed from the parasite surface, or perhaps is shed at levels below the detection limit of this assay.
evidence: Antibody-coated slide assay shows no detectable LIMP trails.

claim: The number of moving and partially moving limp::gfp salivary gland sporozoites was similar to WT.
source: While the CSP trail-based motility analyses failed to flag the motility defect of limp::gfp parasites, live motility assays of salivary gland sporozoites revealed a peculiar feature in this strain: the number of moving and partially moving parasites was similar to WT (Figure 5A)
evidence: Live motility assays show similar proportions of moving parasites.

claim: The speed of limp::gfp salivary gland sporozoites was reduced by more than 35% when quantified by live microscopy.
source: but the speed was reduced by more than 35% when quantified by live microscopy (Figure 5B).
evidence: Quantitative speed analysis shows significant reduction in limp::gfp.

claim: limp::gfp parasites have a higher number with irregular trails and wider circumferences instead of tight, concentric rings typical for WT parasites.
source: Upon closer examination of trajectories of gliding paths, we identified a higher number of limp::gfp parasites with irregular trails and wider circumferences instead of tight, concentric rings typical for WT parasites (sporozoite tracks are visualised by connecting lines between two consecutively tracked positions) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Analysis of gliding trajectories shows different patterns in limp::gfp.

claim: WT sporozoites complete one full circle within a lower number of frames than the slower limp::gfp sporozoites.
source: This means that WT sporozoites complete one full circle within a lower number of frames than the slower limp::gfp sporozoites.
evidence: Analysis of circular movement shows WT completes circles faster.

claim: WT parasites move continuously in a circular fashion following their crescent shape.
source: Typically, WT parasites move continuously in a circular fashion following their crescent shape (Video 1).
evidence: Video microscopy shows continuous circular movement in WT.

claim: limp::gfp sporozoites produce a peculiar 'limp' during movement.
source: limp::gfp sporozoites on the other hand produced a peculiar 'limp' (Video 2)—whence the gene and protein designation is derived.
evidence: Video microscopy shows characteristic limping movement in limp::gfp.

claim: The limping motility of limp::gfp sporozoites is characterised by a failure to detach with the rear end while the front end continues moving forward.
source: This limping motility is characterised by a failure of the sporozoite to detach with the rear end, while the front end continues moving forward thus leading to a transient loss of curvature and a straightening of the parasites, whereby the body size remains unchanged.
evidence: Video analysis shows rear end attachment during forward movement.

claim: limp::gfp sporozoites show an accentuated frequency of cell stretching events.
source: limp::gfp sporozoites show an accentuated frequency of these cell stretching events (Figure 5D–E)
evidence: Quantification of stretching events shows higher frequency in limp::gfp.

claim: Less than 22% of WT sporozoites exhibit one or more limps during 100 s of gliding.
source: While less than 22% of WT sporozoites exhibit one or more limps during 100 s of gliding, 62% of limp::gfp sporozoites limped at least three times during that period (Figure 5D).
evidence: Quantification of limping events shows low frequency in WT.

claim: 62% of limp::gfp sporozoites limped at least three times during 100 s of gliding.
source: While less than 22% of WT sporozoites exhibit one or more limps during 100 s of gliding, 62% of limp::gfp sporozoites limped at least three times during that period (Figure 5D).
evidence: Quantification of limping events shows high frequency in limp::gfp.

claim: The limping effect was specific for C-terminally GFP-tagged LIMP.
source: This effect was specific for C-terminally GFP-tagged LIMP, while both the smaller C-terminal MYC-tag or the N-terminal mCherry-tag supported WT movement and did not produce the staccato movement of limp::gfp (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: Comparison of different tagged lines shows limping only in C-terminal GFP tag.

claim: The smaller C-terminal MYC-tag supported WT movement and did not produce the staccato movement of limp::gfp.
source: This effect was specific for C-terminally GFP-tagged LIMP, while both the smaller C-terminal MYC-tag or the N-terminal mCherry-tag supported WT movement and did not produce the staccato movement of limp::gfp (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: Live motility assays show normal movement in limp::myc.

claim: The N-terminal mCherry-tag supported WT movement and did not produce the staccato movement of limp::gfp.
source: This effect was specific for C-terminally GFP-tagged LIMP, while both the smaller C-terminal MYC-tag or the N-terminal mCherry-tag supported WT movement and did not produce the staccato movement of limp::gfp (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: Live motility assays show normal movement in mcherry::limp.

claim: The average speed of mcherry::limp parasites was similar to WT and faster than that of limp::gfp sporozoites.
source: Consequently, the average speed of mcherry::limp and limp::myc parasites was similar to WT and thus faster than that of limp::gfp sporozoites (Figure 5B).
evidence: Speed measurements show mcherry::limp moves at WT speed.

claim: The average speed of limp::myc parasites was similar to WT and faster than that of limp::gfp sporozoites.
source: Consequently, the average speed of mcherry::limp and limp::myc parasites was similar to WT and thus faster than that of limp::gfp sporozoites (Figure 5B).
evidence: Speed measurements show limp::myc moves at WT speed.

claim: LIMP contains three N-terminal beta sheets and two anti-parallel helices (G60-K83 and K89-N109) at the C-terminus.
source: LIMP contains three N-terminal beta sheets and two anti-parallel helices (G60-K83 and K89-N109) at the C-terminus (Figure 1C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Structural prediction and molecular dynamics simulations define secondary structure.

claim: The structure of LIMP is conserved among all Plasmodium LIMP members.
source: This structure is conserved among all Plasmodium LIMP members (Figure 1B)
evidence: Sequence alignment and structure prediction show conservation.

claim: The WT LIMP protein maintained a stable fold during 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations.
source: The WT protein maintained a stable fold, while LIMP::GFP showed a clear destabilisation of helix 1 (G60-K83) resulting in a kink and a subsequent break of the helix between H71 and Y75 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Molecular dynamics simulations show stable structure for WT LIMP.

claim: LIMP::GFP showed a clear destabilisation of helix 1 (G60-K83) resulting in a kink and a subsequent break of the helix between H71 and Y75.
source: The WT protein maintained a stable fold, while LIMP::GFP showed a clear destabilisation of helix 1 (G60-K83) resulting in a kink and a subsequent break of the helix between H71 and Y75 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Molecular dynamics simulations show helix destabilization in LIMP::GFP.

claim: The stable intra-helical H-bonds were lost in helix 1 (G60-K64, I72-E76 and E73-T77) of LIMP::GFP.
source: Furthermore, the stable intra-helical H-bonds were lost in helix 1 (G60-K64, I72-E76 and E73-T77) and helix 2 (S95-K99) of LIMP::GFP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Molecular dynamics simulations show loss of hydrogen bonds in LIMP::GFP.

claim: The stable intra-helical H-bonds were lost in helix 2 (S95-K99) of LIMP::GFP.
source: Furthermore, the stable intra-helical H-bonds were lost in helix 1 (G60-K64, I72-E76 and E73-T77) and helix 2 (S95-K99) of LIMP::GFP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Molecular dynamics simulations show loss of hydrogen bonds in LIMP::GFP.

claim: The GFP tag occludes the surface area of LIMP helices.
source: In addition, the GFP tag occludes the surface area of LIMP helices, while neither MYC nor mCherry tags interfere with this surface (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Molecular dynamics simulations show GFP blocks access to LIMP helices.

claim: Neither MYC nor mCherry tags interfere with the surface area of LIMP helices.
source: In addition, the GFP tag occludes the surface area of LIMP helices, while neither MYC nor mCherry tags interfere with this surface (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Molecular dynamics simulations show MYC and mCherry do not block LIMP helices.

claim: The loss of structural integrity and solvent accessibility in the GFP fusion protein is likely the cause for the reduced efficiency in detachment and limping motility.
source: The loss of structural integrity and solvent accessibility in the GFP fusion protein is likely the cause for the reduced efficiency in detachment and limping motility.
evidence: Correlation between structural changes and phenotype suggests causation.

claim: LIMP is a novel and key gliding motility factor in the sporozoite.
source: Especially, the near-absence of salivary gland sporozoites in Δlimp mutants suggested that LIMP is a novel and key gliding motility factor in the sporozoite.
evidence: The severe phenotypes in motility and invasion support this conclusion.

claim: LIMP could be involved in the attachment of sporozoites to the substrate.
source: We propose that LIMP could be involved in the attachment of sporozoites to the substrate, and perhaps regulate efficient turnover of attachment sites in gliding parasites.
evidence: Adhesion defects and limping phenotype suggest role in attachment.

claim: LIMP could regulate efficient turnover of attachment sites in gliding parasites.
source: We propose that LIMP could be involved in the attachment of sporozoites to the substrate, and perhaps regulate efficient turnover of attachment sites in gliding parasites.
evidence: The limping phenotype suggests defect in detachment/turnover of adhesion sites.

claim: Gliding motility requires the establishment and dissolution of parasite-host cell contact points.
source: Plasmodium and related apicomplexan parasites move by gliding motility, which requires the establishment and dissolution of parasite-host cell contact points and the ordered turn-over of such adhesion sites (Münter et al., 2009)
evidence: Published studies establish this as a requirement for gliding motility.

claim: TRAP is cleaved by rhomboid protease within the transmembrane domain severing the connection between parasite and host.
source: in the case of TRAP, this is mediated by rhomboid protease cleavage within the transmembrane domain severing the connection between parasite and host (Ejigiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Published study shows TRAP cleavage mechanism.

claim: Δlimp parasites are required for the establishment of initial adhesion contacts with the substrate.
source: Δlimp parasites adhere less to hepatoma cells or glass surfaces implying that LIMP is required for the establishment of initial adhesion contacts with the substrate, thereby affecting the subsequent events of motility and invasion
evidence: Adhesion assays show reduced attachment in Δlimp parasites.

claim: LIMP has an equivalent function to TRAP in establishing adhesion contacts.
source: in that sense, it has an equivalent function to TRAP (Münter et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison of phenotypes suggests similar function.

claim: Strong adhesion forces at the rear end of the sporozoite during gliding can lead to temporal arrest, causing stretching of the parasite when it pulls forward.
source: After attachment to the substrate, continuous parasite motility requires the continuous turnover of adhesion sites. Strong adhesion forces at the rear end of the sporozoite during gliding can lead to temporal arrest, causing stretching of the parasite when it pulls forward (Münter et al., 2009).
evidence: Published study describes this phenomenon.

claim: Unlike Δtrap mutants, the limp::gfp mutant is able to glide, albeit with reduced speed caused by frequent stretching events as a result of a de-adhesion defect at its rear end.
